paras: The lynching of Will Leach took place on the night of August 5-6, 1915, when a mob took Leach, a Black man, from the jail at Dade City, Florida, and hanged him at Trilby. Leach was charged with attacking a thirteen-year-old white girl at Trilby, and his killing was reported nationally by the Associated Press and in a Memphis roundup of nine Black men hanged in the South in a single day.

According to the Associated Press, Leach was charged with attacking a thirteen-year-old white girl at Trilby on June 30, about five weeks before the lynching. He was being held in the jail at Dade City at the start of August.

The Lakeland Evening Telegram reported that about twenty men left Trilby around midnight and reached Dade City about 2 o'clock. The mob attacked the jail and overpowered the jailer, and with his keys in hand it took Leach from his cell within minutes. Leach was driven by automobile to Trilby, where he was hanged in front of the railroad station. The Lakeland paper added that his body was later "filled with bullets," a detail its headline gave as "RIDDLED WITH BULLETS."
No report of an inquest, of arrests of mob members, or of any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named anyone in the mob.

The Associated Press dispatch, datelined Trilby, August 6, ran in Florida and across the country, often in a short form that reduced the event to a jail attack and a lynching "charged with attacking a white girl." Northern dailies frequently printed it beneath the story of Ed Berry, lynched the same day at Shawnee, Oklahoma, and weekly news columns were still carrying it a week later. Florida papers framed the killing as deserved, the Lakeland Evening Telegram headlining "PAID PENALTY FOR USUAL CRIME" and the Pensacola Journal "FLORIDA MOB LYNCHES AN OFFENSIVE DARKEY."

A Memphis roundup published on August 7 set the lynching beside seven legal hangings in Alabama and Mississippi, describing "a crowd of citizens" at Trilby. One version of the roundup said "a crowd, hypnotized with fury" had acted, while the Richmond Virginian opened its copy with "Friday was a bad day for Southern negroes." A separate telegram to the New-York Tribune described "a big mob" that was "Frenzied" over the alleged assault and called Leach only "suspected of the crime." Editorial comment pointed in different directions: the South Bend News-Times contrasted the lynching with a legal hanging in Mississippi, and the Atlanta Jeffersonian wrote that "The crimes deserved death" and blamed the Leo Frank case for distrust of the courts.

In the Black press the lynching appeared in the same Memphis roundup, printed in the Chicago Defender on August 14 under the headline "NINE HUMAN BEINGS HANGED IN SOUTH WITHIN 24 HOURS." Its subhead called four of the deaths legal and the others "Cold Blooded Murders," though the item itself gave the place as "Trinity, Fla." and the victim as "William Leach" and added no new detail. The Denver Star reprinted the Defender item on August 21, crediting the Chicago paper.

Accounts differed on the size of the mob, about twenty men in the Lakeland report and "a big mob" in the Tribune's telegram, and the Lakeland headline said Leach was "HUNG TO TREE" while its text and the wire placed the hanging in front of the railroad station.

accounts.label: Associated Press dispatch from Trilby
accounts.gist: A mob attacked the Dade City jail, overpowered the jailer, brought Will Leach to Trilby and hanged him in front of the railway station; he was charged with attacking a thirteen-year-old white girl there on June 30.

accounts.label: Lakeland Evening Telegram local addition
accounts.gist: About twenty men left Trilby about midnight, reached Dade City about 2 o'clock, took the jailer's keys, carried Leach back by automobile, hanged him and later filled his body with bullets.

accounts.label: Memphis telegram to the New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: A 'big mob' in Trilby, 'Frenzied' over the assault on a thirteen-year-old girl, broke into the jail and hanged Leach, 'suspected of the crime'.

accounts.label: Memphis roundup
accounts.gist: Among nine Black men hanged in the South in one day, 'a crowd of citizens' at Trilby lynched Leach, accused of attacking a 13-year-old girl; carried by white papers and by the Chicago Defender.

framing.detail: The Lakeland Evening Telegram headed its report 'PAID PENALTY FOR USUAL CRIME', and the Pensacola Journal headlined 'FLORIDA MOB LYNCHES AN OFFENSIVE DARKEY'.
Most papers outside Florida ran the AP brief without comment, often beside the Shawnee, Okla., lynching of Ed Berry.
The Memphis roundup set the lynching among seven legal hangings; one version said 'a crowd, hypnotized with fury' acted, and the Richmond Virginian opened 'Friday was a bad day for Southern negroes'.
The Atlanta Jeffersonian counted Florida's lynching among the week's and wrote that 'The crimes deserved death', blaming the Frank case for distrust of the courts.
A South Bend News-Times editorial cited the Trilby lynching as a contrast to a legal hanging staged as a public picnic in Starkville, Miss.
The Chicago Defender ran the Memphis roundup under a headline saying that four were 'Legal, While Other Five Were Cold Blooded Murders'; the Denver Star reprinted it.

conflicts.note: 'Dave City' and 'Trinity' are typesetting variants; the Denver Star reprint of the Defender item reads 'Trilby' (A34).
Spelling variants of one name; every account reports a single victim.
Consistent with the Lakeland account that the mob reached Dade City about 2 o'clock (A1).
